There is no direct contact e-mail address for Customer Support. Please use the online contact form and any responses will be issued via e-mail.

If you have made a request under the Freedom of Information Act or Environmental Information Regulations – the statutory timescale for response is 20 working days following receipt of your request.

If you have made a request in relation to your data rights, for example, a subject access request for personal data – the statutory timescale for response is one calendar month following receipt of your request.

Please note that where personal data is held on our register, it is exempt from the right of subject access under UK GDPR.

Where any personal data is held on record for a registered title, the exemption provided at Schedule 2, Part 1, Paragraph 5(1) of the Data Protection Act 2018 would be engaged.

This states:

“5(1) The listed GDPR provisions do not apply to personal data consisting of information that the controller is obliged by an enactment to make available to the public, to the extent that the application of those provisions would prevent the controller from complying with that obligation.”

Please see the section below titled 'Register information and your data protection rights' for further explanation.

If you have only copied your correspondence to us - we will not respond.

Yours sincerely

Information Rights Team
HM Land Registry

Accessing information held by HMLR on our register of title

To assist you in accessing information held by HMLR, please be aware most of the information held within our registers is open to public inspection and accessible via statutory routes of access. This means that we may be unable to provide access to this information via a Freedom of Information Act 2000 (FOIA) request.

Statutory Routes of Access to information held on Public Registers

The Land Registration Act 2002 is the principal legislation governing land registration in England and Wales. It sets out provisions for keeping a register of title to land and property, and in accordance with Section 66 & 67 of the Land Registration Act, it is a requirement that the Chief Land Registrar makes this information (including any documents held on the register of title) available for public inspection.

How to access information held on our Registers

The information you have requested is available to access under our statutory protocol under section 66 & 67 of the Land Registration Act 2002.

Search for Land and Property

Please visit our website for further information about our registers:

www.gov.uk/get-information-about-property-and-land<http://www.gov.uk/get-information-about-property-and-land>

Official Copies

For information about how to apply for official copies of documents held in relation to registered titles, and information about the types of documents available, please refer to practice guide 11:

www.gov.uk/government/publications/inspection-and-application-for-official-copies/practice-guide-11-inspection-and-application-for-official-copies<http://www.gov.uk/government/publications/inspection-and-application-for-official-copies/practice-guide-11-inspection-and-application-for-official-copies>

Index of proprietors’ names

Under rule 11 of the Land Registration Rules 2003 the registrar is required to keep an index of proprietors’ names which shows for each individual register the proprietor of the registered estate and the proprietor of any registered charge together with the title number. When you search the index of proprietors’ names, you will receive a list of titles that are owned by, or mortgaged to, the name that you have searched against.

For further information about this please refer to practice guide 74:

www.gov.uk/government/publications/searches-of-the-index-of-proprietors-names/practice-guide-74-searches-of-the-index-of-proprietors-names<http://www.gov.uk/government/publications/searches-of-the-index-of-proprietors-names/practice-guide-74-searches-of-the-index-of-proprietors-names>

Section 21 FOIA exemption: Information accessible to the applicant by other means

Where information held on the register of title is available for inspection through these statutory routes of access it is exempt from disclosure under section 21(2)(b) of FOIA.

Section 21 states:

“21 Information accessible to applicant by other means.

(1) Information which is reasonably accessible to the applicant otherwise than under section 1 is exempt information.

(2) For the purposes of subsection (1)—

(a) information may be reasonably accessible to the applicant even though it is accessible only on payment, and

(b) information is to be taken to be reasonably accessible to the applicant if it is information which the public authority or any other person is obliged by or under any enactment to communicate (otherwise than by making the information available for inspection) to members of the public on request, whether free of charge or on payment.”

Therefore, we are unable to provide information held on our register through FOIA, as it covered by this exemption.

Advice and assistance

Under Section 16 of FOIA and in accordance with the Section 45 FOIA code of practice, we have a duty to provide you with reasonable advice and assistance.

Please note that the ICO has previously reviewed HM Land Registry’s use of the section 21 exemption. Relevant decision notices can be accessed here<https://icosearch.ico.org.uk/s/search.html?collection=ico-meta&profile=decisions&query&query=&f.By+authority%7CpublicAuthority=HM%20Land%20Registry&f.By+section%7CsectionOfLegislation=FOI%2021> including IC-173302-N4J1<https://ico.org.uk/media/action-weve-taken/decision-notices/2022/4022883/ic-173302-n4j1.pdf>, FS50685812<https://ico.org.uk/media/action-weve-taken/decision-notices/2017/2172810/fs50685812.pdf> and FER0454056<https://ico.org.uk/media/action-weve-taken/decision-notices/2012/780474/fer_0454056.pdf>.

The ICO has agreed that this position is long established, and the Commissioner is satisfied that section 21 would be engaged for this type of request.

For assistance on how to obtain official copies of documents you can contact our Customer Support Centre by telephone between 8am and 5pm, Monday to Thursday on [phone redacted] or online through our Contact Us<https://customerhelp.landregistry.gov.uk/guide-page-external/?stepid=2b31bc48-eb96-eb11-b1ac-002248413956> form.

Our Customer Support colleagues are trained to handle queries which relate to information that is held on the register of title.

Information about how to apply to inspect or obtain official copies is contained with practice guide 11:

www.gov.uk/government/publications/inspection-and-application-for-official-copies/practice-guide-11-inspection-and-application-for-official-copies<http://www.gov.uk/government/publications/inspection-and-application-for-official-copies/practice-guide-11-inspection-and-application-for-official-copies>

If you need any support completing the application form for official copies or to determine which documents to order, you may contact our Customer Support colleagues:

www.gov.uk/guidance/contact-hm-land-registry<http://www.gov.uk/guidance/contact-hm-land-registry>

You may also refer to our Publication Scheme which includes information about how to access information that is held on the register of title under the heading ‘Request information’:

www.gov.uk/government/organisations/land-registry/about/publication-scheme#request-information<http://www.gov.uk/government/organisations/land-registry/about/publication-scheme#request-information>

Please refer to HMLR’s Transaction Data webpage which contains information in respect of commonly used abbreviations:

www.gov.uk/guidance/hm-land-registry-transaction-data#abbreviations-used-in-transaction-data<http://www.gov.uk/guidance/hm-land-registry-transaction-data#abbreviations-used-in-transaction-data>

If you need any independent advice about individual’s rights under information legislation you can contact the Information Commissioner’s Office (ICO). The ICO is the UK’s independent authority set up to uphold information rights in the public interest, promoting openness by public bodies and data privacy for individuals.

The contact details for the ICO are detailed below. There is useful information on the ICO website which explains the rights of individuals:

www.ico.org.uk/for-the-public<http://www.ico.org.uk/for-the-public>

Please refer to the top tips:

www.ico.org.uk/for-the-public/official-information<http://www.ico.org.uk/for-the-public/official-information/>

Register information and your data protection rights

Data protection law permits HM Land Registry to use personal data for our official purposes.

The lawful basis for HM Land Registry processing personal data under the United Kingdom (UK) General Data Protection Regulation (UK GDPR) is that it is necessary to enable us to perform our public task of the registration of land and property (Article 6(1)(e) of UK GDPR). This is defined in the Land Registration Act 2002.

Paragraph 5 of Schedule 2 Part 1 of the Data Protection Act 2018 provides the following exemption from the specified UK GDPR provisions:

“The listed UK GDPR provisions do not apply to personal data consisting of information that the controller is obliged by an enactment to make available to the public, to the extent that the application of those provisions would prevent the controller from complying with that obligation.”

The Land Registration Act 2002 is the principal legislation governing land registration in England and Wales. It sets out provisions for the keeping of a register of title to land and requirements for its administration by HM Land Registry under a Chief Land Registrar.

The Chief Land Registrar is required by the Land Registration Act 2002 and to make register information (including any documents held on the register of title) available to the public, therefore the following data protection provisions do not apply:


  *   the requirement to provide ‘privacy notices’ to individuals
  *   the requirement to provide personal data in response to subject access requests
  *   the requirement to rectification
  *   the requirement to comply with requests to erasure (right to be ‘forgotten’)
  *   most of the principles of UK GDPR


Please visit our website for further information about our registers:

www.gov.uk/get-information-about-property-and-land<https://www.gov.uk/get-information-about-property-and-land>

For further information in relation to your rights and how HMLR processes personal data please refer to our Personal Information Charter:

www.gov.uk/government/organisations/land-registry/about/personal-information-charter<http://www.gov.uk/government/organisations/land-registry/about/personal-information-charter>




HM Land Registry’s purpose is to protect your land ownership and provide services and data that underpin an efficient and informed property market. Our vision is: “A world-leading property market as part of a thriving economy and a sustainable future”.

We welcome correspondence in English and Welsh.

Sirs/ Ma'ams,

I need to correct a date I have used in earlier correspondence about Great
House Farm / Tŷ Mawr, Llandough, titles WA231076 and WA240304.

I had treated 1983 as the year the two titles were merged. That was wrong.
HM Land Registry’s own letter of 23 March 2026 (Lisa Griffiths, ref
N610CGV) separates the two acts.
1982–83 was first registration of two live titles, not a merger.
30 November 1982: application to first-register WA231076. The Court of
Appeal later treated BP Properties Ltd as registered proprietors of “the
farm” from November 1982.
23 February 1983: application to first-register a second title, WA240304.
26 March 1983: Mary Williams died. On the family’s case, notice of those
applications did not reach us until after her death, while the family was
in mourning. She had no window in which to object. The family was not in a
position to use any window that arrived after that.
Those two titles remained separate through first instance.
24 July 1986: Hollis J. Both titles were still live. The judgment language
treats Great House Farm as one holding. It had not been one holding on the
register. On the family’s case it had not been one holding since the 1877
split: Parcel A (house, buildings, garden/yard and about 10 acres, the
Thomas/Williams line) and Parcel B (the eastern fields retained by Bute and
later WGR/BP).
2 February 1987: application to amalgamate the two titles. WA240304 was
then closed and registration continued under WA231076. That is the merge.
It was made after the 1986 ruling and before the Court of Appeal gave
judgment on 31 July 1987.
So 1983 is silent first registration of a second title while Mary was still
in Parcel A, or had only just died. 1987 is the administrative merger,
carried out while the appeal was still open.
This was not a dispute about a single land parcel that BP already owned.
Mary was on Parcel A, which the family says she owned, with occupation on
that house parcel running in the family from at least 1667. BP, and WGR
before it from 1949, were the neighbouring interest on Parcel B. From 1949
onwards the family’s case is that those neighbours ran a decades-long
series of tenancy offers, “whole farm” wording, possession orders and the
1974 letters to make her occupation of her own parcel look permissive, and
to make both parcels look like one estate they had acquired. They never
produced a conveyance of Parcel A. What they had was an unfounded claim
that her occupancy was permissive.
Please treat any earlier letter from me that said the titles merged in 1983
as corrected by this email. The dates that matter are:
1982/83 — first registration of two titles, without the occupier being
heard;
24 July 1986 — first-instance judgment describing one farm while two titles
still stood;
2 February 1987 — amalgamation, before the appeal ended;
31 July 1987 — Court of Appeal.
Yours faithfully,

Sion Buckler
Refs where relevant: N610CGV; 260919-6726246; titles WA231076 and WA240304.

I have spent approximately twenty years researching this matter and have
assembled a substantial body of documentary, archival, court, Land Registry
and family evidence. I am not asking ICR to determine ownership itself. I
am asking it to review whether HM Land Registry properly investigated and
answered the complaint put before it, whether it addressed the evidence I
supplied, and whether the reasons given for its conclusion adequately
explain how the disputed registration was accepted and subsequently
maintained.
1. The underlying family ownership claim

The family's position is that our historic Parcel A was a distinct parcel
of land around the farmhouse and woodland and that our underlying freehold
interest was never lawfully extinguished.

My grandmother, Mary Williams, consistently asserted ownership of the
family parcel. The documentary history presently available to me raises a
substantial question as to whether Parcel A was ever conveyed to Western
Ground Rents in the manner subsequently assumed.

There is an important distinction between:

   - the family-occupied Parcel A surrounding the farmhouse; and
   - the eastern agricultural Parcel B which was the subject of the later
   agricultural tenancy arrangements.

The 1939 revised agricultural tenancy documentation which I have located
appears to concern Parcel B and its associated land. The accompanying plan
does not appear to include the family-occupied Parcel A.

This raises a basic documentary question:

What instrument actually conveyed Parcel A to Western Ground Rents, if it
was ever conveyed to them at all?

I have not yet obtained a document which satisfactorily answers that
question.
2. The 1928 / 1938 / 1939 documentary sequence

The present reconstruction begins with the 1877 arrangements involving the
Marquess of Bute and Daniel Thomas & Son and the subsequent quarrying
arrangements.

My understanding from the evidence presently assembled is that the relevant
quarrying arrangements were completed by 1928 and that the family
thereafter continued in occupation of Parcel A as its own land.

The later 1938 conveyancing from the Bute estate to Western Ground Rents
therefore requires close examination as to precisely what land was conveyed.

This is particularly important because the 1939 revised agricultural
tenancy record naming Western Ground Rents as landlord appears, from its
plan, to concern Parcel B rather than Parcel A.

That record was brought to my attention by the clerk for Llandough Town,
who directed me to the archive material shortly before his retirement
earlier this year.

If Parcel A was not conveyed to Western Ground Rents in 1938, and was not
included in the 1939 agricultural tenancy, the subsequent legal narrative
by which the family's occupation came to be treated as permissive requires
considerably more examination than HM Land Registry's present response
appears to have given it.
3. The successive attempts to characterise the family occupation as
permissive

The historical evidence reveals a sequence of events which I believe needs
to be examined as a whole rather than in isolation.

These include:

*1949* — an attempted tenancy arrangement concerning Parcel B which appears
to have sought to include my grandmother in the tenancy and thereby connect
her occupation of Parcel A with the agricultural tenancy of Parcel B;

*1951* — the disappearance of important family papers, including the
family's title documentation, which my grandmother reported as stolen;

*1955* — possession proceedings in which the language concerning the “whole
farm” requires comparison with the actual definition of the agricultural
holding and its separate parcels. The order also expressly excluded the
“house and garden” and referred to my grandmother's “condition and
resistance”;

*1959* — an offer of a tenancy of the farmhouse and garden, which my
grandmother rejected while continuing to assert an ownership claim;

*1962* — a possession order concerning the farmhouse and garden, the legal
effect and subsequent enforcement history of which require examination;

*1965* — a further attempt to place “Mrs Williams” into a weekly tenancy,
again rejected;

*1974* — an ownership action was adjourned; leave to enforce the 1962
possession order was obtained but the warrant was not pursued; and BP
subsequently relied upon the two letters of 31 October 1974 as establishing
a licence relationship.

The family interpretation is that these were not independent, isolated
events but a succession of attempts to convert or present an allegedly
proprietary occupation as permissive.

I appreciate that this is an interpretation requiring documentary testing.
That is precisely why I believe HM Land Registry should have engaged with
the underlying documents rather than treating the later registered position
and the 1987 Court of Appeal judgment as effectively resolving the matter.
4. The 1987 judgment does not answer the documentary provenance question

A particularly important part of my complaint concerns the way HM Land
Registry has relied upon *BP Properties Ltd v Buckler* [1987] EWCA Civ 2.

I do not dispute that this was an important Court of Appeal decision.

However, the case concerned the adverse-possession and possession issues
concerning the farmhouse and garden. The Court considered the
registered/paper-title position relied upon by BP, the previous possession
proceedings and the legal effect of the 1974 letters upon the character of
Mrs Buckler's occupation.

The judgment itself records that Mary Williams had asserted that she had a
title to Great House Farm through her grandfather and believed that
documents existed establishing that title, but that such documents were not
produced.

The point is therefore not that the Court of Appeal “never touched title”.
It plainly considered BP's registered/paper-title position.

The point is narrower and, in my view, fundamental:

The 1987 judgment is not itself the conveyance, plan, root deed or other
documentary instrument establishing how the woodland and the family's
historic Parcel A entered BP's registered title.

Nor did it adjudicate the validity of Forest of Cardiff's separate 1994
acquisition of the woodland.

I am concerned that HM Land Registry's present response treats the 1987
judgment as though it answers a documentary provenance question which it
did not determine.
5. The 1969 conveyance and 1971 abstract

HM Land Registry has also told me that BP supplied a title chain extending
back to 1969.

That raises another substantial documentary issue.

There were only thirteen years between the 1969 conveyance and BP's first
registration in 1982.

The 1969 conveyance from Western Ground Rents to BP Pension Trust therefore
requires examination as to exactly what proprietary interest was being
conveyed.

I understand the later title documentation to recite the 1969 conveyance as
a root document, while the 1971 abstract refers to the 1962 possession
order and an OS plan.

If the underlying title to Parcel A was never conveyed to Western Ground
Rents, the critical question is how an asserted interest arising from
possession proceedings could subsequently be treated as though it were
documentary title to the parcel itself.

The 1971 abstract is therefore particularly important.

HM Land Registry's own correspondence has recorded that such an abstract
was lodged. The 30 July 2026 schedule of surviving first-registration
documents does not identify the 31 December 1969 conveyance itself, nor
does it resolve the evidential gap concerning the 1971 abstract.

I am continuing to pursue those underlying records.
6. The 1982–83 registrations

My principal concern is that BP may have registered not the family's actual
historic Parcel A, supported by a lawful root title, but a later
constructed or “synthetic” parcel derived from the succession of
possession, tenancy and licence documents which had been used to
characterise the family occupation as permissive.

I use “synthetic parcel” as a description of the issue I am investigating,
not as a statement that this is already legally established.

The essential question is:

What precise land did BP apply to register in 1982–83, what documentary
instrument entitled BP to register that land, and did that land correspond
to the land actually conveyed to BP's predecessors?

The later amalgamation of the BP titles is also significant because what
may have originated as separate parcels or interests appears subsequently
to have been brought together within the registered estate.

It is necessary to establish whether that process merely recorded an
existing lawful title or whether it caused an underlying proprietary
boundary to disappear within a later registered estate.
7. HM Land Registry's response

HM Land Registry has now maintained that it was correct to register the
land and has relied, in part, upon the 1987 judgment.

I respectfully submit that this does not answer the complaint.

An administrative conclusion that a registration was “correct” cannot
itself reconstruct a missing conveyance, establish the precise boundary of
land conveyed decades earlier, or demonstrate that a later registered
proprietor had documentary title to a distinct parcel where the underlying
conveyancing remains disputed.

Nor does the existence of the 1987 judgment establish the documentary
provenance of WA735527 or the validity of the separate 1994 transfer to
Forest of Cardiff.

I am particularly concerned that HM Land Registry appears to regard its
reliance upon the 1987 judgment as effectively validating the 1982–83
registration, when the registration itself pre-dated the judgment.

The chronology matters.

The registration came first.

The litigation came afterwards.

I therefore cannot see how a later judgment concerning possession and
adverse possession can, without further analysis, resolve whether the
earlier registration accurately represented the documentary title existing
at the date of registration.
8. Notification and my grandmother's death

Another issue which requires consideration is notification.

To my knowledge, the family was not notified that BP had applied to
register the relevant land in 1982.

My grandmother died on 14 March 1983, shortly after the first registration
and within the period in which the registration would have been capable of
being challenged had she known of it.

She had spent decades rejecting attempts to characterise her occupation as
permissive and consistently maintaining an ownership claim.

The fact that she died shortly after the registration is not itself proof
of wrongdoing. It is, however, a material chronological fact when
considering whether she had a meaningful opportunity to challenge the
registration and whether HM Land Registry appropriately considered the
notification history.

I ask the ICR to consider whether HM Land Registry has adequately addressed:

   - what notice was given of the 1982 application;
   - to whom it was given;
   - what information was supplied to the persons potentially affected;
   - whether any competing ownership claim was disclosed by the applicant;
   - and what records exist showing how HM Land Registry assessed those
   matters.

9. Possible fraud, concealment and institutional involvement

Through my research I have also identified matters which I consider may
warrant investigation for possible fraud, deliberate concealment,
misrepresentation, mistake and institutional involvement.

I want to be precise about this.

I am not asking the ICR to find that fraud occurred.

I am asking the ICR to consider whether HM Land Registry adequately
investigated evidence raising those questions, particularly where the
evidence concerns missing historic documents, the distinction between
Parcel A and Parcel B, the provenance of the 1969 title, the 1971 abstract,
the 1982–83 registrations and the subsequent amalgamation of titles.

I have deliberately distinguished established documentary facts from
matters which remain hypotheses requiring investigation.

There are also serious questions concerning the destruction or absence of
historical records and the later treatment of the land. Those matters are
being pursued through separate archival and documentary channels.
10. The human and public-interest dimension

This is not merely an abstract registration dispute.

My grandmother was a disabled widow and amputee who maintained an ownership
claim to the family land through decades of litigation and repeated
attempts to characterise her occupation as permissive.

The family was ultimately removed from the property in 1988. The historic
farmhouse, which had been our family home and which we believe had
significant architectural and historic importance, was subsequently
demolished.

I was a child when we were removed.

Family possessions and historic material were lost or dispersed, while the
land was subsequently developed and altered.

The family's connection with the site is recorded as extending back to the
seventeenth century, and I was born at Great House Farm.

There are also wider heritage and archaeological questions concerning the
site and its subsequent development, which I am investigating separately.

I mention these matters because they explain why I have continued the
investigation for approximately twenty years and why the accuracy of the
underlying land record matters so profoundly to my family.

My professional background is in military cyber and electronic warfare, and
much of my research has involved reconstructing fragmented documentary
histories and identifying discrepancies between records. I have approached
this as an evidential investigation rather than simply as a family
grievance.
11. Why I am approaching the ICR

I therefore ask the ICR to review HM Land Registry's handling of my
complaint and, in particular, whether it:

   1.

   adequately investigated the distinction between historic Parcel A and
   Parcel B;
   2.

   adequately considered the 1938 conveyance and 1939 revised tenancy plan;
   3.

   adequately addressed the documentary provenance of the 1969 conveyance
   and the 1971 abstract;
   4.

   adequately examined the precise land comprised in the 1982–83
   registration applications;
   5.

   relied upon the 1987 *BP v Buckler* judgment for a proposition which the
   judgment itself did not determine;
   6.

   adequately considered the chronology whereby the 1982–83 registration
   preceded the 1987 judgment;
   7.

   adequately investigated the notification given to persons asserting
   ownership of the land;
   8.

   adequately addressed the missing or unavailable historic documents and
   the evidential gaps I have identified;
   9.

   adequately considered the evidence I supplied rather than simply
   reaffirming the existing registered position; and
   10.

   provided reasons sufficient to explain why, notwithstanding those
   unresolved documentary questions, HM Land Registry considers that no
   mistake or registration error occurred.

I am not asking the ICR to adjudicate the family's ultimate title claim.

I am asking for an independent examination of whether HM Land Registry's
investigation and reasoning were adequate, proportionate and properly
responsive to the evidence and issues actually raised.
12. Documents and evidence

I can provide the relevant correspondence with HM Land Registry, the
response to my MP, registration material, historical conveyancing, court
records, archival plans, family evidence and other documents relied upon in
my complaint.

I also maintain a detailed chronology of the matter, including:

1916 — agricultural tenancy;

1928 — completion of the relevant quarrying arrangements;

1938 — Bute / Western Ground Rents conveyancing;

1939 — revised agricultural tenancy and plan;

1949 — tenancy attempt;

1951 — missing/stolen title documentation issue;

1955 — possession proceedings;

1959 — farmhouse and garden tenancy offer;

1962 — possession order;

1965 — further tenancy attempt;

1969 — Western Ground Rents → BP Pension Trust conveyance;

1971 — abstract and plan material;

1974 — ownership proceedings, possession enforcement history and licence
letters;

1975 — BP Pension Trust → BP Properties transfer;

1982 — first registration;

1983 — subsequent registration and title dealings;

1987 — *BP Properties Ltd v Buckler* Court of Appeal judgment;

1988 — final removal from the farmhouse and demolition; and

1994 — subsequent acquisition of the woodland by Forest of Cardiff.

The chronology is significant because it demonstrates why I do not consider
the 1987 judgment, standing alone, capable of answering the earlier
registration question.
13. What I am asking for

I respectfully ask the ICR to accept this as a request for independent
review of HM Land Registry's handling of the complaint.

In particular, I ask that the reviewer consider whether HM Land Registry
has actually answered the documentary questions raised, rather than merely
reaffirming the registered position.

I would also ask that the underlying Land Registry records relevant to the
1982–83 registration, notification, supporting title documents, plans, the
1969 conveyance and the 1971 abstract be considered where they remain
available.

I am not seeking a finding against individual Land Registry staff.

I am seeking an independent assessment of whether the institution's
handling of this matter has been adequate and whether the reasons given for
refusing to recognise a possible mistake are properly supported by the
underlying record.

The issue remains live because the disputed land is now being dealt with
through subsequent titles and, in the case of the woodland, is presently
subject to a proposed disposal by Forest of Cardiff.

I therefore respectfully ask the ICR to consider this matter on the basis
of the documentary chronology and evidence rather than treating the
existence of the current register as dispositive of the historical question.

I am willing to provide a structured evidence bundle and chronology to
assist the review.

Yours faithfully,

Sion Buckler (Ret'd Sergeant)

Hello,

I would like to share a public documentary archive and historical research project: Great House Farm Wiki (Ty Mawr).

Website: [Insert Great House Farm Wiki Link]

The archive documents the 150-year history of Great House Farm in Llandough-juxta-Penarth, South Wales. It brings together primary records from Glamorgan Archives, tithe apportionments, historical Ordnance Survey maps, lease instruments, and family records.

Key highlights of the repository include:
- A structured Two-Parcel Analysis of the land and historical titles.
- Primary evidence records cross-referencing Bute Estate and Western Ground Rents tenancy documents.
- A machine-readable index and evidence library for legal and local history research.

If you are interested in South Wales history, land archival records, or local heritage, please feel free to explore the wiki and share it within your network.

Best regards,
Bob

Dear Sion Buckler,

Thank you for your email received into our enquiries system 8th September.  Please find below answers to your questions in turn.  Please note that prices quoted are without VAT based on the fact that you are in Patagonia.

**26 May 2026 (2026/2370)**
1. 1974 demolition petition, Llandough juxta Penarth — ref or not held.
There is not a petition held within our collection. You would need to know who the petition was submitted to in order to search for any further reference to it.  If it was submitted to the planning authority there may be mention in the Planning Committee minutes and reports – see point 6 below.

**29 May 2026 FOIA/EIR (2026/2372)**

2. Williams/Buckler as owners, tenants, or reporters of the 1880 floor discovery.
One source of information about ownership would be rate books. UC/73/1 is a rate book for 1882 – this is the nearest we have to 1880.  A search of this (and later volumes UC/73/1-5 covers 1882-1902 and then UDPE/T/30 and UDPE/T/32 cover dates after 1900) could be undertaken by staff on your behalf at a charge of £50 which would include copies of relevant entries.

3. Gaps / missing volumes / withdrawals 1950–1989.
We have never had a full set of records that would show the full tenancy/ownership history of Great House / Ty Mawr Farm. With all historical research of this nature, it is necessary to piece together information from surviving records that have been deposited with us.  There are not any records that have been withdrawn from our collections that would have provided additional information to this search for the period 1950-1989.

4. Why the fabric was not scheduled before 1988 (or “Cadw holds this; we hold nothing”).
Not held in our collections – suggest contacting Cadw and the Royal Commission on the Ancient and Historical Monuments of Wales.

5. Internal preservation assessments.
As above - suggest contacting Cadw and the Royal Commission on the Ancient and Historical Monuments of Wales.

6. Planning files for this acreage / demolition / Church View Close — file refs, not class names.
We do not hold planning files (it is possible some files may still be held by the Vale of Glamorgan Council Planning Department), but we do hold copies of the Planning Committee minutes and reports.  Mary Buckler started looking at the Planning Committee minutes and reports on her last visit to the searchroom on 13th August.  The document references to start with for these would be DCVG/C/4/36/76-77 and DCVG/C/4/36/94 these are for the planning applications 1989/01396/OUT and 1992/00671/RES.  It is possible that the minutes may make reference to any earlier applications or discussions.  A search of these records and anything else that they lead to could be carried out by staff at a charge of £50 to include copies of any relevant pages found.

7. When the known archaeology was raised in planning.
If any record of this is in our collections it would appear in the Planning Committee records described above in point 6.

8. EIAs / HER / developer briefs 1980–1990.
The HER for Wales is searchable via the Heneb website: Historic Environment Records (HER) - Heneb<https://heneb.org.uk/historic-environment-records-her/>.  You could also contact the Glamorgan Gwent Archaeological Trust to see if they have any relevant information.

**27 July / 5 August 2026 (2026/3309)**
9. DB/E/1–2 Stewart survey / Cedfin.
This was consulted and photographed by Mary Buckler in our public searchroom.  If you would like to receive copies of the pages relating to Ty Mawr this would be two images (one from DB/E/1 the survey and one from DB/E/2 the terrier).  Total cost £17 (£13 for the first image in the order and £4 for the next image).

10. Lambert Williams–Bute agreements 1818–1835 (not the D160 maps already seen).
Not held. Possibly at the National Library of Wales?

11. Material related to NLW D219.
Not held – this is a National Library of Wales reference: Llandough manorial leases and agreements, - National Library of Wales Archives and Manuscripts<https://archives.library.wales/index.php/llandough-manorial-leases-and-agreements> You should contact the NLW for access or copies.

12. D153/4–8 1876 limeworks severance — not seen.
Not held – this is a National Library of Wales reference: Deeds relating to premises in p. Llandough, co. Glam., comprising a dwelling house adjoining the churchyard, 1811 (D153/1-2), land (19 ..., - National Library of Wales Archives and Manuscripts<https://archives.library.wales/index.php/deeds-relating-to-premises-in-p-llandough-co-glam-comprising-dwelling-house-adjoining-churchyard-1811-d153-1-2-land-19>.  You should contact the NLW for access or copies.

13. DXJF/64/27–32 full sketch bundle — notes seen; confirm sketches and refs.
We believe that the specific references within the bundle 27-32 that would be of interest to you are items DXJF/64/30-31: sketch of former layout of part of village of Llandough-juxta-Penarth by Mrs. Nancy Buckler of great house farm, Llandough, with notes c1950 [1 card, 1 paper]. Is that what you have already seen?  Other items in the bundle do not relate to Llandough.

14. DCOWHS on Buckler of Penarth (not DCO/WHS/2).
DCOWHS/2 is the only part of the DCOWHS (Cowbridge and District Local History Society) that relates to Buckler of Penarth. No other records held.

15. Exact ref of the Nov 1877 counterpart already photographed; separate July 1877 counterpart?
I think the items described below have been discussed previously – are these what you are seeking?  Please confirm and we can provide a quote for producing copies if required.

Document reference

  *   DBDT/1/3
Title

  *   Adamsdown Square leases from the trustees of the will of the late Marquess of Bute<https://glamorgan.epexio.com/en/records/DBDT/1-110/1>. Lease to Mr John Williams
Level of description

  *   Item
Date

Extent

Document reference

Title

Level of description

Date

  *   Nov 1877
Extent

  *   1 parchment; plan in margin

16. Cardiff RDC records for this farm.
No records found. The area was not covered by Cardiff Rural District Council but rather Penarth Urban District Council.

17. DRA 418–420 / DRA 5/31 if this site.
Neither of these are complete document references from our collection.  Perhaps you could check these references or let us know what you think they should be and we will be happy to search our catalogue.

18. UDPE/S/1/68.
This was viewed by Mary Buckler on 6th August and is a set of plans for a pair of semi-detached houses on the road between Dinas Powys and Llandough. If you would like copies of these plans 5 images will be required at a charge of £20.

19. Penarth estate/tithe/OS/boundary plans of the house plot (not Cowbridge 1924/38).
The relevant estate map would be the Bute Estate survey which is referred to in point 9 above.  You can view the tithe map online here: Tithe Maps of Wales<https://places.library.wales/viewer/4622411#?cv=&h=95&xywh=10530%2C8509%2C3549%2C1196> along with the accompanying apportionment: Tithe Maps of Wales<https://places.library.wales/viewer/4542756#?cv=1&h=95&xywh=-507%2C-68%2C2508%2C897>.  Many historic Ordnance Survey maps can also be viewed online, for example through the National Library of Scotland website: Map Finder - with Outlines - National Library of Scotland<https://maps.nls.uk/geo/find/#zoom=15.3&lat=51.45225&lon=-3.20017&layers=101&b=1&z=0&point=51.44624,-3.20044&i=135196558>.

20. WGR / Mountjoy / BP Pension Trust / BP Properties papers.
The only relevant papers we have are those mentioned in point 5.4 in my email of 7th September: collection reference D696 – book of plans and rental books for land owned by Western Ground Rents Ltd c1938-1944.  A search of these records could be carried out on your behalf at a charge of £50.

21. Associated bundles stored separately.
All catalogues have been searched for your enquiry.

22. Uncatalogued / recent deposits 1875–1988.
A search of our accessions database, which records all records received into our collection even if they haven’t yet been catalogued, has not revealed any additional records.

23. Photography for copies to Patagonia — rules.
Please find attached the digital photography order form which applies wherever you are based.  As mentioned above, prices quoted do not include VAT due to your location.  You need to sign and agree to the declaration on the order form.

24–29. DBDT10/19 and 10/20 identification of Daniel Thomas; Bute–Thomas search at Llandough juxta Penarth; quarry/lime/reversion instruments (poor-rate occupation already seen); later title; research cost.
These points were answered in my email of 7th September.

These points were answered in my email of 14th September.

We hope that this information is of use to you.  We will respond to other outstanding emails in due course.

Dear Heneb: The Trust for Welsh Archaeology,
I am writing to request access to recorded information concerning the March 1983 fire at the former Glamorgan-Gwent Archaeological Trust (GGAT) warehouse in Swansea, particularly the reported destruction of archaeological finds, excavation records and photographic
 material from Llandough, together with records concerning the subsequent custody, preservation, transfer and integrity of archaeological records relating to Great House Farm (Tŷ Mawr), Llandough.
I recognise that Heneb is an independent private company limited by guarantee and registered charity rather than a body ordinarily subject to the Freedom of Information Act 2000.
However, Heneb now maintains the statutory Historic Environment Records for Wales on behalf of the Welsh Ministers. Sections 194 and 195 of the Historic Environment (Wales) Act 2023 require the Welsh Ministers to maintain publicly accessible Historic Environment
 Records, including information concerning archaeological investigations and their findings.
I therefore ask that this request be considered under any applicable statutory information-access regime, including the Environmental Information Regulations 2004 insofar as Heneb considers that it falls within their scope.
If Heneb considers that the EIR do not apply to any or all of the information requested, please state that expressly and identify the legal basis for that position. I would nevertheless be grateful if Heneb would consider the request voluntarily as an information-access
 request, particularly where the information forms part of, or supports, the statutory Historic Environment Record or associated archaeological archive maintained on behalf of the Welsh Ministers.
I have copied Cadw and the Royal Commission on the Ancient and Historical Monuments of Wales because the request concerns the statutory HER system and records said to have been transferred or accessioned into the National Monuments Record of Wales.
The request is for existing recorded information only. I am not asking Heneb to create a new report or undertake fresh archaeological interpretation.
Purpose and evidential context
This request arises from a wider forensic examination of the surviving documentary record concerning Great House Farm (Tŷ Mawr), Llandough.
Two companion forensic critiques, dated 21 September 2026, have been prepared concerning respectively Cadw and GGAT/Heneb. They are not presented as proof of dishonesty, bad faith, corruption or deliberate destruction. Rather, they identify a series of documentary
 gaps, inconsistent records and questions which cannot properly be resolved without access to the underlying primary records.
In particular, the GGAT critique identifies questions concerning the Trust's historical roles as archaeological adviser, contractor, investigator, curator and record-holder, and concerning the provenance and subsequent custody of the 1990 Great House Farm
 assessment and associated material.
The purpose of this request is therefore to establish, from the records themselves, what material existed, what was lost, what survived, where it was held, when it was transferred, and whether the present HER and archive accurately represent the historical
 record.
The two distinct archaeological areas at Llandough
For the avoidance of doubt, I ask that the following be treated as separate investigations.
1. Llandough Farm / Roman villa area south of St Dochdwy's church
GGAT undertook excavation in this area in 1978–79, with the HER identifying event GGATE001109 as "Llandough Farm". The associated site record concerns an Iron Age/Roman villa complex with later early-medieval burial activity.
2. Great House Farm (Tŷ Mawr) area north of St Dochdwy's church
GGAT undertook an archaeological assessment/evaluation of Great House Farm in 1990, followed by the substantially larger Cotswold Archaeological Trust excavation in 1994.
These should not be conflated in the records or in any response to this request.
Part A — March 1983 warehouse fire
I have identified contemporaneous newspaper reports concerning the March 1983 fire at the GGAT Swansea warehouse.
Those reports state that substantial quantities of archaeological material were destroyed and specifically identify finds from Llandough among the losses. They also report the destruction of a photographic studio/darkroom and a substantial quantity of photographic
 material.
I therefore request:
1. Any surviving inventory, catalogue, accession register, storage list, box list, find list, archive schedule or other contemporaneous record identifying archaeological material held at the Swansea warehouse immediately before the fire.
2. Any surviving inventory, assessment or other record identifying material from the 1978–79 Llandough Farm excavation which was destroyed, lost, damaged or rendered unrecoverable in the fire.
3. Any records identifying Llandough photographic material lost in the fire, including, where recorded:

original negatives;contact sheets;prints;transparencies/slides;photographic registers or catalogues;site photography logs; andduplicate or working copies.

Dear Ret'd Sergeant Sion Buckler,



Thank you for your enquiry in which you asked for the information concerning the existence, provenance, transfer, retention, destruction or disposal of records relating to Ty Mawr / Great House Farm.



Your request has been handled under the Freedom of Information (FOI) Act 2000. The FOI Act gives you the right to know whether we hold the information you want and to have it communicated to you, subject to any exemptions which may apply.



I can confirm that The National Archives holds some information relevant to your request. We are pleased to be able to provide some of this information to you.



Our response



The initial response from our records enquiries team looked for the four terms (“Great House Farm”, “Ty Mawr”, “Llandough” or “Cedfin”) within the PRO and RW series and did not find any relevant information. We have now tried those terms and the further twelve terms that you have specified in a wider catalogue search. We have provided the results of our search below.



The crux of your query is local land ownership dispute in Glamorgan and the demolition of some buildings by a private company; generally speaking, these are not matters dealt with by central government and we would not expect to see anything within our collections. As such, there would have been no records to transfer. The exception is the court case relating to BP properties, which generated some papers. Links to the catalogue pages for these records can be seen below.



There are likely to be records of the farm in the 1940s as part of the National Farm Survey series but these cannot all currently be searched online by farm.



We are unable to conduct this research on the archival collections on your behalf without charging fees to conduct research on your behalf (Paid Search). A public authority is allowed to charge fees under section 9 of the Freedom of Information Act and within this section of the Act it states: "provision is made by or under any enactment as to the fee may be charged by the public authority for the disclosure of the information" (S9(5) FOIA).



The Public Records Act (1958) enables a statutory instrument to be made setting out the fees which may be made in connection with the supply of information from The National Archives. The prices we charge are set out by our Fees Regulations<https://www.legislation.gov.uk/uksi/2025/1243/made>.



If you are interested in paying for research to be conducted on your behalf, then details of our Paid Search service and other options for paying for research are available here: Paying for research - The National Archives<https://www.nationalarchives.gov.uk/help-with-your-research/paying-for-research/>



If you would prefer to conduct this research yourself then you may find the following research guide to be of assistance: National Farm Survey of England and Wales 1941-1943 - The National Archives<https://www.nationalarchives.gov.uk/help-with-your-research/research-guides/national-farm-survey-england-wales-1941-1943/>

I am not asking the Senedd to determine a private property dispute or to decide legal questions that properly belong before the courts. My concern is the conduct, decision-making, record-keeping and accountability of public bodies responsible for heritage protection, planning and local government.

The surviving evidence presents a series of unusually important questions.

Great House Farm was professionally surveyed by the Royal Commission on the Ancient and Historical Monuments of Wales in 1974. In December 1988, Cadw was considering the building for emergency spot-listing, with a contemporary report stating that inspectors were due to visit and consider the case. The European Commission of Human Rights records that the Convention application had been introduced on 3 May 1988; BP obtained possession on 29 November 1988; demolition began on 6 December 1988; and the application was not registered by the Commission until 12 December 1988.

The evidence therefore establishes a very compressed sequence in which emergency heritage protection was being considered, domestic interim relief was refused, possession was obtained and the building was then destroyed within days.

That chronology does not, by itself, establish coordination, deliberate suppression or unlawful conduct. It does, however, warrant investigation.

There are several specific questions which I believe require answers from an authority independent of the present local authority:

  1.  What information and records were actually considered by Cadw when the 1988 spot-listing decision was made?
  2.  Was the 1974 RCAHMW architectural survey considered, and if not, why not?
  3.  What communications took place between Cadw, South Glamorgan County Council, BP Properties Ltd, the courts and any other public bodies during the critical period immediately preceding demolition?
  4.  What consideration was given by the local planning authority to the available statutory powers of preservation in circumstances where demolition was imminent?
  5.  Why was the building destroyed before there could be an independent retrospective architectural examination of the fabric?
  6.  How should the later archaeological evidence, including the discovery of approximately 1,026 burials in 1994, be understood in assessing the historic significance of the site and the adequacy of the earlier decision-making?   7.  A 1989 planning document appears to describe the site as having formerly contained Great House Farm “(a listed building)”. I ask that this apparent discrepancy be investigated and reconciled with the 1988 Cadw decision.
  8.  What records relating to these decisions still exist, where are they held, and have reasonable steps been taken to preserve and disclose them?

I am particularly concerned that the destruction of the physical building in December 1988 permanently removed primary architectural evidence which could otherwise have been examined independently.

I also ask the Senedd to consider the wider public-interest question: whether the present mechanisms for accountability are adequate where a historic building is destroyed during a period of rapidly developing legal, planning and heritage proceedings and significant questions remain about what information was available to decision-makers.

I would therefore ask the Petitions Committee to consider accepting a petition on this subject and, where appropriate, referring the matter to the relevant Senedd committee or committees for investigation. I would also welcome consideration of whether an independent public inquiry, committee inquiry or other form of external investigation would be appropriate.

I am prepared to provide the underlying documents, chronology, court material, heritage records, planning documents and correspondence supporting these questions.

I am not asking the Senedd to adopt my conclusions. I am asking that the evidence and unanswered questions be examined independently and that the relevant public bodies be required to account for what they did, what they knew, and what records exist.

Please confirm the appropriate route for submitting this formally to the Senedd and whether the material can be referred to the Petitions Committee for consideration.

Thank you for your considered response.

I understand and accept that the Committee does not have a remit to adjudicate upon an individual dispute, determine whether a historical decision was lawful, or direct Cadw to reopen a particular case. My submission was deliberately framed so as not to ask the Committee to do any of those things.

I would, however, respectfully clarify one point, because I am concerned that the nature of the request may have been characterised more narrowly than intended.

The attached report expressly states that it is not a legal challenge, a forensic proof of wrongdoing, a complaint seeking adjudication, or a demand for reversal of the 1988 decision. Its stated purpose is historical record correction, archival explanation and administrative acknowledgement. In particular, it asks for an explanation of why almost none of the records concerning the 1988 assessment survive, whether that reflects the applicable record-retention arrangements, and whether the surviving independent evidence should be properly reflected in the permanent public record.

The central issue therefore extends beyond the merits of the individual 1988 listing assessment.

Cadw's 2026 FOI response confirms that an assessment took place, but that only two exterior photographs now survive; the assessment report, reasons for refusal, site notes, internal recommendations and consultation correspondence are no longer available. The report does not assert that this proves wrongdoing. Rather, it identifies a straightforward public-administration question: how can the adequacy and evidential basis of an irreversible public heritage decision be understood or scrutinised when the underlying administrative record no longer survives?

That seems potentially relevant to the Committee's stated function of scrutinising the administration and accountability of Welsh Government and associated public bodies, even if the Committee cannot itself determine whether the 1988 decision was correct.

I am therefore not asking the Committee to investigate the Buckler family's historical dispute with BP, adjudicate upon the 1988 decision, or direct Cadw to reverse anything. The specific administrative questions raised in the report are instead:

  1.  What record-retention arrangements applied to the 1988 assessment?
  2.  Why do the assessment report, reasons, site notes and consultation records no longer survive?
  3.  Were the records destroyed under an applicable retention policy or other authority, and were they considered for transfer to the appropriate archival institution?
  4.  Is the present position consistent with Welsh Government/Cadw expectations for the preservation of records concerning significant heritage decisions?
  5.  Are current arrangements sufficient to ensure that comparable heritage assessments, particularly where a building is under imminent threat of demolition, are properly documented and retained?

These are not questions that require the Committee to determine the rights of either party to the original dispute. They concern administrative practice, institutional record-keeping and the ability of the Senedd and the public to scrutinise decisions taken by public bodies. The report specifically asks Cadw to explain the archival position and review its current record-keeping practices for this reason.

I would therefore be grateful if the Committee could reconsider whether the broader administrative and accountability issue falls within its scrutiny function, even if the Committee cannot examine the underlying individual dispute.

If the Committee considers that it nevertheless cannot engage with the matter, I would appreciate clarification as to which Senedd or Welsh Government scrutiny, oversight, archival or complaints mechanism is considered appropriate for raising a documented concern about the absence of the administrative record of a historical Cadw decision and the implications this has for public accountability.

For completeness, I should also emphasise that the report itself deliberately recognises the limits of the surviving evidence. It does not claim that Cadw acted unlawfully or in bad faith, and it expressly acknowledges that the absence of the 1988 working papers means that the assessment cannot now be reconstructed definitively.

My objective is therefore quite limited: to ensure that the surviving evidence is preserved, that the archival gap is properly explained, and that the public record accurately distinguishes what is established from what can no longer be verified.

I hope that clarification assists, and I would be grateful if you could confirm whether the Committee is able to consider the matter from that wider public-administration and accountability perspective.

Kind regards,

Dr Wigley,

This is a supplement to the complaint re-served on 20 September, not a
chaser. I do not expect a reply before the stage-one response. It adds
seven matters under the existing headings at section 7, and one addition to
the outcomes at section 9, set out at the end.

The public interest is engaged alongside my family's. Great House Farm
stood beside the Grade I church at Llandough, was recorded by the Royal
Commission in 1974, sat within a known archaeological site, and was
described in the post-demolition planning record as a "county treasure". I
do not ask Cadw to treat the 1994 discoveries as knowledge it had in 1988.
They show what was lost; the pre-1988 record is the measure of Cadw's
process.

On my family's account and the contemporary press report, protection was
being sought in the first days of December 1988 and the house was
demolished almost immediately afterwards. I do not ask Cadw to determine
responsibility for the demolition. The grievance is narrower: protection
was sought at the critical moment, and Cadw cannot now show what it
considered.

1. The adopted development plan (matter A)

The planning officer's report on application 89/01396/OUT records that the
supporting information to Policy H.2 of the East Vale Local Plan "states
that buildings on the site should be retained, however were unfortunately
demolished a little while ago." I do not say this bound Cadw or required
listing. I ask:
(a) was Cadw aware of it in December 1988;
(b) did the planning authority draw it to Cadw's attention; and
(c) if neither can be established, will Cadw say so expressly.

2. The search undertaken on 21 May (matters D and F)

Mr Weatherhead wrote that he had asked a colleague to search other paper
files, "including the Welsh Office files", and would write again with the
result, while fairly warning that some files had quite likely been
destroyed. I have not received that letter. Please confirm whether the
search was carried out, which series were searched, what was found, and
whether Cadw regards the ATISN 27021 response of 11 June as its report of
that search.

3. The meaning of "YYY" (matter J)

Cadw has given two accounts of the marking — that the buildings were
"marginally below the bar for listing" (21 May) and that the building did
not meet the criteria (10 July) — and one inference, that it did not meet
the criteria "as it was not included on the list" (29 July). I ask for one
settled meaning, the documentary source for it, and, if there is none, a
statement to that effect.

4. The retention period (matter J)

Your email of 27 August said that no records of the historic retention
arrangements are available, and that the three-year period is what current
colleagues advised from their knowledge of the systems then in place. I ask
only that the complaint response confirm expressly that this is an account
of general practice, not evidence that the Great House Farm file was in
fact destroyed after three years.

5. Professional archaeological knowledge of this site before December 1988
(matter C)

On 22 September 2026 Amgueddfa Cymru disclosed to me, under FOI 2026-032,
its collections records for two accessions from this site. The first,
82.44H, is the material from the Glamorgan-Gwent Archaeological Trust's
excavation of 1979 on land formerly part of Great House Farm, carried out
in advance of housing development. The museum's records give the findspot
as ST 168 733, the donor as Wales & West Housing Association Ltd, and the
published report as Owen-John 1988. The accession runs to several hundred
entries and includes Roman coins, samian, glass, a bone scabbard slide and
querns, together with medieval pottery and ironwork.

This is not archaeology discovered after the event. By the time Cadw
considered this building, the site had been professionally excavated, the
finds had been accessioned by the national museum under a 1982 accession
number, and the excavation report had been published. I therefore ask, as
an addition to matter C:
(a) whether Cadw held, or had access to, the 1979 excavation record or its
published report when it considered the buildings in 1988;
(b) whether that material was drawn to its attention by GGAT, the planning
authority or the Royal Commission; and
(c) if neither can now be established, that Cadw say so in terms.

I do not say this material required the building to be listed. I say that
the conclusion recorded in December 1988, that the site was not of
sufficient archaeological interest, was reached against a professional
record that already existed and is still held by the national museum today.

6. The National Museum attribution (matter H)

The GGAT assessment of August 1990, which Cadw supplied to me on 21 May,
states that "it is likely that some medieval ironwork which is held by the
National Museum of Wales was discovered under the rear wing c 1880 (RCAHMW

The museum's disclosure allows that sentence to be tested, and the position

7. Correcting the record (matter H)

Dear Mr Buckler

Thank you for your request for an internal review of Amgueddfa Cymru's response to your Freedom of Information request concerning a reported archaeological discovery at Great House Farm, Llandough.

I have now completed my review of the handling of your request, including the searches undertaken and the concerns raised in your request for review.

Having reviewed the original request, the searches conducted and the response provided, I am satisfied that the request was handled appropriately and that reasonable and proportionate searches were undertaken in those locations where information falling within the scope of the request would reasonably be expected to be held.

In your request for review, you suggest that additional searches should have been undertaken using a wider range of terms and concepts, including references to Roman burials, military burials, cavalry burials, human remains, horse remains and other archaeological terminology. I have carefully considered this point. However, when assessing whether information is held for the purposes of the Freedom of Information Act 2000, the relevant issue is not whether every conceivable search term has been used, but whether the authority has undertaken searches that are reasonable and proportionate in the circumstances and reasonably likely to identify relevant information if held.

Your request concerned a specific reported discovery at a named location. Accordingly, the location identified in the request was used as the primary search criterion. Searches were undertaken across Amgueddfa Cymru's information holdings where records relating to acquisitions, accessions, archaeological finds, provenance information and associated correspondence would reasonably be expected to be held. This included collections management systems, accession records, archived documentation, shared electronic records and other organisational record repositories.

Records identified through those searches were reviewed by collections staff and the FOI team to determine whether they related to the reported discovery described in your request. As the search methodology was location-based rather than focused on a particular object type, archaeological period or interpretation, it was reasonably likely of identifying relevant records regardless of whether associated material had been recorded as Roman, medieval or otherwise.  I have therefore considered your suggestion that later historical accounts may have inaccurately described the nature, date or attribution of the reported discovery. I am satisfied that this possibility would not have affected the outcome of the searches undertaken.

I have also considered whether broader keyword searches would have been appropriate. Given the scale and diversity of Amgueddfa Cymru's collections and records, generic terms such as "horse", "burial" or "skeleton" would retrieve large volumes of records relating to many different sites and periods and would not provide a reliable or proportionate means of locating records relating to a specific reported discovery at a named location. I am satisfied that the location-based search strategy adopted was the most appropriate and proportionate approach.

The searches undertaken did not identify any records relating to:
* the acquisition, accession, donation, transfer or deposit of a visor, lance, helmet, armour or related objects associated with the discovery described in your request;
* associated human or animal remains connected with that discovery;
* reburial records relating to that discovery; or
* excavation reports, discovery reports or watching-brief records relating to the discovery described in your request.

Having reviewed both the scope of the original request and the searches undertaken, I am satisfied on the balance of probabilities that, if information relating to the reported discovery were held by Amgueddfa Cymru, those searches would have been likely to identify it.

You also raised concerns regarding the reference in the original response to other archaeological records identified during the course of the searches. Those records were reviewed and were not considered to relate to, or otherwise be associated with, the reported discovery described in your request. However, I can confirm that this aspect has been subject to further consideration and a separate response will be issued in relation to those records.

I therefore uphold the original conclusion that Amgueddfa Cymru does not hold recorded information falling within the scope of your request.

This concludes Amgueddfa Cymru's internal review process. If you remain dissatisfied, you may complain to the Information Commissioner's Office under section 50 of the Freedom of Information Act 2000.

I am not asking your Council to revisit Mr Egan's answer of 14 June 2026.

Glamorgan Archives in 2002, and I am pursuing those there.

What I am asking about is what that answer did not cover. Llandough
Community Council is a public authority under Schedule 1, Part II,
paragraph 7(b) of the Freedom of Information Act 2000. The Act applies to
the recorded information set out below generally; the Environmental
Information Regulations 2004 apply in addition to any part of it that is
environmental information.

PART ONE — REQUEST FOR RECORDED INFORMATION

1. Whether the Council holds any recorded information created after the
2002 deposit — minutes, correspondence, reports, emails, photographs or
files of any kind — concerning Great House Farm (Ty Mawr) / Church View
Close, the village green in front of St Dochdwy's including registered
green VG 41, or the roadside verge by the churchyard wall.

2. Whether the Council holds any photographs, postcards or images of the
farm, the barn, the green or the church surroundings, of any date.

3. Whether the Council holds any recorded information showing what, if
anything, transferred to it from Penarth Town Council at the 1982
reorganisation, and any recorded information identifying where the pre-1982
Llandough community records were deposited.

If the answer to any of these is that no such information is held, I would
be content with a short statement to that effect — but I do need it stated.
Section 1(1)(a) of the Act requires the Council to confirm or deny whether
the information is held.

Section 10 (and regulation 5 of the EIR) allows twenty working days from
receipt, which on my request of 20 September 2026 I calculate as 16 October
2026.

If the Council is refusing, section 17 (and regulation 14) requires a
written refusal notice identifying the exemption or exception relied on;
section 17(7) requires the Council to give particulars of any complaints
procedure it operates, or to state that it has none, and to notify me of my
right to apply to the Information Commissioner; and regulation 11 gives a
right to an internal review of any refusal under the EIR.

"We have nothing more to add" does not meet those requirements. If the

Wigley,

I sent you the formal complaint below on 17 September 2026. I have since
established that it never reached you.

It was addressed to [email redacted], which rejected it — my mail server
recorded "message blocked… the address couldn't be found or is unable to
receive email." A copy addressed to [email redacted] also failed, that
domain having been decommissioned. The only addresses that accepted it were
[email redacted] and [email redacted].

The latter is Cadw's visitor-services contact centre operated by Transport
for Wales, which replied on 18 September under reference #628635887 to say
it had been passed to their complaints manager. That is plainly not the
right destination for a complaint about a 1988 listing assessment, and I do
not want it pursued there. I would be grateful if that reference could be
closed.
I should add that [email redacted] has now rejected correspondence from me on
three separate occasions — 23 January, 29 August and 17 September 2026. If
that address is still published anywhere as a contact point for Cadw, it
may be worth someone looking at.

I am therefore re-serving the complaint on you directly, unchanged. The
text below is exactly as sent on 17 September. Please treat it as received
today, and please let me have a complaint reference.

Two points of clarification, so that nothing is misread.

First, this is not a further Freedom of Information request. I accept your
email of 4 September, in which you confirmed that Cadw has released all the
records it holds concerning the 1988 listing decision, and I am not asking
you to produce documents you have already said no longer survive. I am
conscious that I have made requests to Cadw and to the Welsh Government
Information Rights Unit since May of this year and that they have been
answered. My complaint is not that records are being withheld. It is about
what can properly be established from the evidence that does survive, and
about whether Cadw's account distinguishes clearly enough between "we
cannot now establish this" and "this did not happen."

Second, I am treating this as stage one of the Welsh Government complaints
process, not stage two. You directed me to that process on 4 September. I
have copied the Complaints Advice Team so that the complaint is logged and
dated, but I am not asking for a formal investigation yet. I would rather
Cadw had the first opportunity to answer it. I will only escalate if the
stage one response does not engage with the ten matters set out at section
7 below.

One further matter, which I raise in the hope it is useful rather than as
part of the complaint. Cadw's 1988 file is lost, but Cadw did not
correspond with itself. Any letters Cadw wrote in 1988 about this building
were received by the Royal Commission, by Vale of Glamorgan Borough
Council, and by the Glamorgan-Gwent Archaeological Trust, and copies may
survive in their files even though yours have gone. I have requests with
the Royal Commission and with Heneb which cover exactly that. If either
produces Cadw correspondence you no longer hold, I will send it to you, as
I said I would in August. I would rather Cadw's own record of this was
complete than score a point off its being incomplete.

I look forward to a complaint reference and to a substantive reply.

Yours sincerely,

Sion Buckler (Ret'd Sergeant)

Dear Calli,

Further to my email of 8 September 2026 concerning Great House Farm / Tŷ
Mawr, Llandough, I attach a formal schedule of the records I am seeking, so
that the request is easier for Heneb to work through and to allocate
internally. I have also completed your online enquiry form, so the request
is in your preferred channel.

I appreciate a response would not fall due until 6 October, so this is not
a chaser. It is to put the detail in one place and to clarify the basis of
the request.

On your note of 22 May. You are right that Heneb, as a limited company, is
not a public authority under the Freedom of Information Act 2000, and I do
not pursue that. Two separate points remain, and I would welcome Heneb's
position on each.

First, the Environmental Information Regulations 2004 apply on a different
test — regulation 2(2) reaches bodies carrying out functions of public
administration relating to the environment, or under the control of a
public authority. If Heneb considers it falls outside that, please say so
expressly with brief reasons, so that I can direct the request elsewhere.

Second, and independently, the Historic Environment Record is a statutory
record: sections 194 and 195 of the Historic Environment (Wales) Act 2023
require the Welsh Ministers to maintain an HER for every local authority
area and to make it available for public inspection, and Heneb keeps the
south-east Wales record on their behalf. I therefore ask in the alternative
that this be treated as a request for access under that regime and under
Heneb's own policy.

Two things that will make this easier. If any item is too broad, please
tell me which and I will narrow it rather than have the whole request
refused. And if Heneb can supply, as a first step, simply a schedule or
index of the records it holds for this site — without copying them — that
would let me target the rest precisely and save your staff considerable
time. I am content to inspect material by appointment at Baglan or at the
HER, and any reasonable copying or staff-time charge can be notified to me
in advance for approval.

Two small administrative points. Please confirm which legal entity now
holds the records and functions formerly of Glamorgan-Gwent Archaeological
Trust Ltd, and who within Heneb handles access requests of this kind.

Finally, since my correspondence in May was framed more formally: my
purpose is documentary. I am reconstructing the record of a farm my family
occupied for generations, and I would far rather do that with Heneb's help
than around it.

I should say plainly that I have read GGAT's December 1993 notification to
the Vale of Glamorgan that Condition 18 had not been complied with, and the
recommendation that a Breach of Condition Notice be issued. Whatever else
is in dispute about this site, that was the Trust doing its job properly,
and I am grateful for it.

Thank you in advance for your time in this matter,

Regards,

Sion Buckler (Ret'd Sergeant)
Royal Signals Cyber/Electronic Warfare Professional and Life Member
