MP Doughty,

Further to my letter earlier, I would like to narrow what I am kindly
asking of you, and to correct one other thing.

My letter asked which document brought the former farmhouse and garden at
Great House Farm into BP Properties Limited's registrable estate. HM Land
Registry has in fact already answered that, and I should have acknowledged
it. Its letters of 23 March and 19 April 2026 identify a conveyance dated
19 November 1982 for title WA231076, and a conveyance dated 23 May 1975 for
title WA240304. I will apply to HM Land Registry directly, on form OC2, for
copies of those deeds and their plans. I am not asking you to obtain them
for me.

Two questions remain. Both concern inconsistencies within HM Land
Registry's own correspondence, rather than anything I am asserting. So that
you need not open any attachments, I have set out the relevant passages
verbatim in the annex below, with dates and authors.

1. The 1971 abstract of title. The letter of 19 April 2026 states twice
that an abstract of title dated 1971 was lodged with the applications. The
letter of 30 July 2026 sets out a complete schedule of the documents held
on both first-registration files — thirty items for WA231076 and thirteen
for WA240304 — and no abstract of title appears anywhere on either list.
Was the abstract lodged; does the list of documents lodged (item 17 on that
schedule) record it; and if it was lodged, what became of it?

2. The conveyance of 31 December 1969. Both operative conveyances recite
the same root of title: a conveyance dated 31 December 1969 between Western
Ground Rents Limited and The British Petroleum Pension Trust Limited. That
deed does not appear on the 30 July schedule either. Was it produced to the
registry at first registration; does the list of documents lodged record
it; and if it was not produced, on what evidence was the recital accepted
as establishing the root of title?

Both questions can be answered by examining a single document which HM Land
Registry confirms it holds and describes as open to public inspection. I am
not asking it to reopen BP Properties Ltd v Buckler [1987] EWCA Civ 2, to
determine ownership, or to revisit any decision it has made. A written
answer to those two questions is all I am seeking.

I can also withdraw one request from my earlier letter. I asked that the
surviving records be preserved; that is no longer necessary, as HM Land
Registry has confirmed the documents will remain on file.

My earlier request to meet you stands, but it is not pressing. These two
questions can be dealt with in writing.

Yours sincerely,

Sion Buckler

PS - see attached images. I purchased all deeds I could, but the primary
one is inaccessible for purchase as of today. I have raised this issue with
A.I.

ANNEX — VERBATIM EXTRACTS FROM HM LAND REGISTRY CORRESPONDENCE
All under reference N610CGV. Originals available on request.


A. Letter of 23 March 2026 — Lisa Griffiths, HM Land Registry Wales Office

"It appears Ty Mawr Farm was originally registered under two different
title numbers, WA231076 and WA240304. These two titles were amalgamated.
Title WA240304 was closed as a result of the amalgamation and the
registration continued under title WA231076."

"We received an application for registration on 30 Nov 1982. The
application was submitted by Linklaters & Paines of Barrington House, 59/67
Gresham Street, London, [postcode redacted], to register BP properties Limited of
Britannic House, Moor Lane, London, EC2 as proprietor. The land was
conveyed to BP Properties Limited by a Conveyance dated 19 Nov 1982 made
between (1) The British Petroleum Pension Trust Limited, (2) BP Trustees
Limited and (3) BP Properties Limited"

"We received an application for registration on 23 February 1983… The land
was conveyed to BP Properties Limited by a Conveyance dated 23 May 1975
made between (1) The British Petroleum Pension Trust Limited, (2) BP
Trustees Limited, (3) BP Properties Limited."


B. Letter of 19 April 2026 — Charlotte Takeuchi, Assistant Land Registrar
(stage one complaint response)

On the standard applied:

"In unregistered conveyancing, title is ultimately based on the estate
owner's right to be in possession of the land or to receive the rents and
profits of it. Showing a full documentary title commencing with a good root
of title that is at least 15 years old should normally establish this right
and is sufficient for land registration purposes."

On the abstract of title, in relation to WA231076:

"Our files show an abstract of title listed dated 1971 was lodged with the
application for first registration. This is effectively a summary of deeds,
documents and events which show a person's title to unregistered land."

On the abstract of title, in relation to WA240304:

"Again, our files indicate that we had sight of a copy of a 1971 abstract
of title."

On the root of title recited in the 19 November 1982 conveyance:

"The recitals clause (preamble) to that Conveyance states 'The Vendors are
seised in fee simple in the premises described in the First Schedule hereto
(hereinafter called "the premises") upon the Trusts referred to in a
Conveyance dated 31 December 1969 and made between Western Ground Rents
Limited of the one part and the Vendors of the other part..' It is clear
therefore that the applicant (BP Properties Limited) could show a good root
of title and that The British Petroleum Pension Trust acquired the land in
1969."

On the root of title recited in the 23 May 1975 conveyance:

"The recitals clause to that Conveyance states 'The Vendors are seised in
fee simple upon the trusts referred to in a conveyance dated the thirty
first day of December One thousand One hundred and sixty nine [sic] and
made between Western Ground Rents Limited of the one part and the vendors
of the other part.'"


C. Letter of 25 May 2026 — Harbinder Gill, Land Registrar (stage two, final
response)

"HM Land Registry operates a two-stage internal complaints procedure, and
this constitutes our second and final response. It is not possible to ask
anyone else in HM Land Registry to review the matter again."

"We will not be commencing the process of rectification or formally
referring the dispute."


D. Letter of 30 July 2026 — S. G. Haste, HM Land Registry Wales Office

"After an investigation of our files, we can confirm that the following
documents are available."

The letter then lists thirty documents held for title WA231076 and thirteen
for title WA240304. Item 17 of the WA231076 list reads:

"A13- DL-List of documents lodged with first registration"

Neither list includes an abstract of title of any date, nor a conveyance
dated 31 December 1969.

The letter concludes:

"We can confirm that all these documents are held on file and will remain
on file. They are all open to public inspection if require copies of them."

texts.gm-1a0b7ad7c7c10d58:
*MP *Doughty,

Further to the correspondence from Mr Iain Banfield, and my earlier email,
I am writing again to be sure, placed on record, is the central issue which
HM Land Registry's response still does not answer.

I appreciate that HM Land Registry is not a court and that it cannot simply
reopen a Court of Appeal judgment. That, however, does not answer the
separate question of whether the land registered in 1982/83 was correctly
identified and supported by the documentary title then placed before the
Registrar.

Mr Banfield's response relies heavily upon *BP Properties Ltd v Buckler*
[1987] EWCA Civ 2. That judgment post-dated the registration by
approximately four years. It records BP Properties Ltd as having become
registered proprietor of the "whole farm" in November 1982 and then
determines the later adverse-possession dispute concerning the farmhouse
and garden. It does not, however, determine whether the 1982
first-registration application had itself correctly included the farmhouse
parcel in BP's documentary title, or whether the registration had
mistakenly conflated two historically separate parcels.

That distinction is fundamental.

My family's parcel — the former farmhouse, garden and curtilage, which I
refer to as the *House Plot* — was historically distinct from the adjoining
eastern agricultural land. The documentary history I have obtained
indicates that these areas were not simply one undifferentiated proprietary
parcel.

The 1916 agricultural tenancy is one important document because it embraced
both areas. But that is not the end of the conveyancing history. The
earlier 1877 Daniel Thomas & Son instrument, and the arrangement
subsequently acted upon when the quarrying ceased in 1928, point to a
separate proprietary interest in the House Plot.

I have the 1938 conveyance from the Marquis of Bute to Western Ground
Rents, and the revised 1939 version of the 1916 tenancy, and it did not
convey or demise the House Plot at all: the actual 1938 conveyance, the
1939 tenancy and their plans need to be examined by you lot too, not just
me. Indeed, the 1987 judgment itself records that the alleged yearly
tenancy commencing in 1949 has not been produced in the proceedings. Its
geographical extent therefore remains unproved. Not withstanding it may
pertain to the parcel to the east we leased and defaulted on, not our
freehold parcel. Furthermore my nan expressly rejected the 1949 tenancy and
attempt to make her occupancy of our parcel permissive in such a way, but
expressly rejecting it while asserting her ownership claim of her parcel.

It's adolescent of everyone to keep having a meltdown and failing to
compute the simplicity of the fact Mary Williams asserted she owned her
parcel. And WGR saught possession of theirs, east of it. Western Ground
Rents, already described in UK Parliament as praying on elderly and being
abhorrent and scrupilous, clearly tried to make Mary's occupany appear
permissive in 1949 and the 1955  proceedings.

The 1987 judgment records that and the 1962 proceeding, after the
agricultural tenancy was terminated, as Western Ground Rents obtaining a
1955 possession order for the "whole of the farm". Crucially, however, when
that order was enforced on 4 July 1955, possession was taken of all
parts *except
the farmhouse and garden*. The judgment gives the immediate reason as Mrs
Mary Buckler's condition and her strong resistance to leaving the
farmhouse. Ambiguity which is later misinterprited and clearly an early
attempt at making her occupancy of her parcel appear permissive.

WGR subsequently brought a *fresh action in 1962 specifically against Mr
and Mrs  Buckler for possession of the farmhouse and garden and mesne
profits*, resulting in the possession and mesne-profits order of 11
December 1962. The judgment records that this order was not enforced before
1974.

That sequence matters.

If the two areas had genuinely always constituted one undifferentiated
proprietary estate subject to the same right of possession, it is difficult
to understand why possession of the agricultural land was recovered in 1955
while the farmhouse and garden were left occupied and a separate possession
action had to be brought in 1962.

I therefore ask that this fact not be retrospectively converted into an
assumption that the 1955 "whole farm" wording necessarily comprised the
House Plot in the same legal sense as the agricultural land.

The statutory effect attributed by the Court of Appeal to the 1955/1962
proceedings cannot itself establish title to a different, historically
separate parcel which was never actually comprised in those proceedings.

The possession orders were orders for possession and associated relief.
They were not conveyances. They did not retrospectively create a
documentary chain of title where none existed, nor did they by themselves
determine the geographical extent of an underlying freehold documentary
title.

That is especially important in light of the sequence of events recorded in
the 1987 judgment. WGR's own successive proceedings and selective
enforcement distinguished the agricultural land from the farmhouse and
garden in practical terms, whatever the later interpretation of the
expression "whole farm".

There is a further point which I believe HM Land Registry has not addressed.

In 1949, according to the history now being assembled, Mrs Mary Williams
was offered a tenancy of the farmhouse and garden which she rejected
because she asserted ownership. The 1987 judgment itself confirms that she
was offered a tenancy of the farmhouse and garden by Western Ground Rents
and refused it. It also records that she had come to believe she had a
title through her grandfather and that documents existed which supported
that claim.

Thus there was plainly a known dispute over the House Plot long before
first registration.

The 1974 proceedings and letters must also be put in their proper place.
The Court of Appeal held that the 1974 letters operated as a licence,
notwithstanding that Mrs Buckler had never expressly accepted them, and
held that her possession thereafter was no longer adverse.

I am not asking HM Land Registry to disregard that decision.

Despite it being clear to any sane, reasonable person to see that, given
the evidence, the 1974 order was not truly quashed due to the licence
letters, which came afterwards and were backdated. Made out to a non
existent Mrs Buckler. And quashed the case within minutes of Mary being
notified of them, with no ample opportunity to respond. Albeit she actually
did in writing. And asserted her ownership and challenged BP in a public
newspaper. Not withstanding BP couldn't give something they don't own i.e.
permissive occupancy.

This permissive occupancy followed by a conversion is a racket. Look at the
pattern;

1955 permissive occupancy ploy > 1969 conveyance (WGR to BP Pension Trust
Ltd)

1974 permissive occupancy ploy > 1975 conveyance (BP Pension Trust to BP
Properties Ltd)

Nor am I asking the Land Registry to even acknowledge the fact court
clerked notified the press who all decended on the scene, covered the story

The applicable statutory framework in 1982/83 was the Land Registration Act
1925 and the Land Registration Rules 1925.

The Rules expressly contained provisions dealing with first registration,
including *rule 20, requiring the applicant to deliver the original deeds
and documents relating to the title which were in its possession or control*.
The operation of that rule in the first-registration context is confirmed
in *Walker v Burton*, where the High Court described the requirement in
those terms.

The Rules also contained a specific provision headed *"Examination of title
by Registrar"* and provisions concerning searches and enquiries by the
Registrar.

This means that the question cannot simply be reduced to "Land Registry
registers what it is given".

   4.

   proposed registration plan generated a requisition or further enquiry;
   5.

   uncertainty as to the extent of the documentary title; and
   6.

   the Registrar's own records contain any warning, requisition, note,
   correspondence or other indication that the separate House Plot issue was
   considered.

Registration Rules 1925 contained a specific power in *rule 14* dealing
with "registration in error", including registration of too large a part of
a title, and explained that the registrar had an express power to rectify
registration arising from mistake.

mistake in the register*, and gives as an example a title being mapped to
include land for which the registered proprietor has no documentary title.

possession can amount to lack of proper care. I appreciate that this is

retrospectively as the law of 1983. It is nevertheless directly relevant to
the distinction HM Land Registry now draws between a genuine registration
mistake and a mere disagreement about the title boundary.

questions about the extent of a registered title. Again, I cite this as an

   Council, and who has custody of its historic records?
   2.

   Was Llandough Community Council consulted on application 89/01396/OUT
   and/or the subsequent reserved-matters application? If so, please provide
   the consultation requests, replies, minutes and associated correspondence,
   or confirm specifically that no such material is held.
   3.

   Please provide the full planning decision notice dated 3 September 1992,
   including all conditions, rather than the approved drawings alone.
   4.

   Please confirm whether Vale holds the 1994 Cotswold Archaeology
   site/excavation plans and the relevant Ideal Homes development layout
   plans. Please also confirm whether the Council has ever undertaken or
   commissioned a plan-to-plan comparison showing the excavation area against
   the approved development footprint.
   5.

   Please identify the officer or officers responsible for assessing the
   1989 application against the information then available concerning the 1988
   demolition and HER/SMR record 2038s, including the entries "None",
   "Disused" and "Not known".
   6.

   Please confirm what planning, enforcement, conservation/heritage,
   archaeological, consultation, photographic and correspondence records
   remain for the site and where they are presently held.
   7.

   Given the issues raised by my FOI/EIR correspondence and the corporate
   complaint of 17 September 2026, please ensure that surviving records
   concerning Great House Farm / Tŷ Mawr, including Community Council records
   where they remain identifiable, are preserved pending resolution of these
   matters. I am particularly concerned that records should not disappear
   simply because responsibility has passed from one office-holder to another.
   8.

   Please confirm whether there was a formal handover, inventory or records
   transfer when Mr Egan retired, and whether any such documentation records
   the location of material concerning Great House Farm, planning
   consultations, or the 1988 demolition.
   9.

   Finally, if the Council considers that any aspect concerning Mr Egan's
   conduct as Community Council Clerk falls outside the Vale's jurisdiction,
   please identify the proper route and responsible body rather than simply
   closing that part of the complaint.

I am deliberately separating evidence from inference. I am not alleging
that Mr Egan's retirement was caused by my FOI requests, nor am I alleging
that any individual deliberately concealed records. The timing, however, is
sufficiently relevant that the Council should establish what happened to
the records at the point responsibility changed. The immediate issue is
capable of being answered objectively: what records exist, what was known
to the authority, what checks were carried out, what decisions were made,
and where the missing documents are now.

Please treat this as a formal request for a written governance/records
response and address each numbered question individually. It should be read
alongside FOI/EIR reference 00210772 and my correspondence of 17–18
September 2026.

Regards,

Thank you for your recent correspondence which I am responding to on behalf of the Leader, concerning Great House Farm/Church View Close, the removal of a commemorative tree and your communications with Councillor Carroll.
I have considered the matters you have raised.
As you are aware, I have previously responded to your concerns regarding Councillor Carroll's lack of response to your correspondence. Having reviewed those concerns, I concluded that the matter did not fall within the Council's Corporate Complaints Policy and I did not identify any basis for further action under the Members' Code of Conduct process. The Council has no mechanism by which it can compel an elected member to respond to correspondence from a constituent and, accordingly, the Council's consideration of that aspect of the matter is concluded.
Please note that the Leader is not responsible for the conduct of Members other than those with her own political group
I note that your recent correspondence extends beyond the issue of Councillor Carroll's responsiveness and raises a broader range of concerns relating to historical land ownership, planning and heritage matters associated with Great House Farm/Church View Close, together with a request for information regarding the removal of a commemorative tree.
In relation to the tree, I am making enquiries to establish whether the Council holds any records which may assist in answering your question regarding its removal. This is being dealt with by the Information Governance Team, I have copied in the FOI unit email domain. If relevant information is held by the Council, I will advise you accordingly. Equally, if no such records are held, I will confirm that position.
In respect of the wider matters raised in your correspondence, it is important that I clarify the scope of the Council's role. The Council is not able to determine disputed ownership of land, revisit historical legal proceedings, adjudicate upon competing title claims, or investigate allegations of fraud or other criminal conduct. Those matters fall within the jurisdiction of the courts, HM Land Registry, the police and other external bodies as appropriate.
Whilst I appreciate the strength of feeling reflected in your correspondence and recognise the significance that these matters have for you and your family, the Council must limit its involvement to those issues which fall within its statutory functions and responsibilities. Any response provided by the Council will therefore be confined to matters upon which it may properly comment and any information which it may hold.
The FOI team will write to you further once enquiries regarding the tree have been completed.

From: Sion Buckler <[email redacted]>
Sent: 10 September 2026 15:23
To: Burnett, Lis (Cllr) <[email redacted]>; Leader <[email redacted]>

Subject: Escalation — Llandough ward member silence: Great House Farm / Church View Close and removal of commemorative tree

Councillor Burnett,

I write to you as Leader of the Vale of Glamorgan Council because the elected member for Llandough, Councillor George D. D. Carroll, has not answered a sequence of written enquiries spanning more than six months. I am going above him for that reason alone. I am not asking you to adjudicate the historic title dispute. I am asking that a constituent with a documented family interest in the ward receive a reply that the ward member has declined to give.

I understand that elected members do not have a line manager in the employment sense. Councillor Carroll is Leader of the Conservative Group. You are the political head of the authority. After the ward member and the Monitoring Officer, you are the proper next addressee.

Why I am writing to you rather than waiting further

1. Councillor Carroll has not sent a single substantive reply to me at [email redacted]<[email redacted]>.
2. On 27 July 2026 I filed a formal complaint about that silence (copied to him, Democratic Services and the Monitoring Officer).
3. On 12 August 2026 Victoria Davidson, Monitoring Officer, wrote that the matter fell outside the Corporate Concerns and Complaints Policy and that she had not identified a Code of Conduct breach. That determination did not require him to respond. It left the original questions unanswered.
4. I followed up with the Monitoring Officer on 12 August, 21 August and 24 August 2026. The position did not change.
5. I copied Councillor Carroll again on 28 August 2026 (joint letter with Stephen Doughty MP). Still no reply from him.

The questions he has not answered include a simple, current, ward-level one: who removed the tree my great-grandfather planted to mark the family’s claim, as recorded in the Collection of Wales / archival image. That is a local enquiry a ward member can signpost to Parks, Highways, Planning or the landowner. It is not a request that he retry BP Properties Ltd v Buckler.

From his public output, Councillor Carroll appears to concentrate on blocked drains, potholes and similar highway defects. Those matters matter. The correspondence I sent him is of a different character: heritage, planning and enforcement records, the 1988 demolition of Great House Farm (Ty Mawr), now Church View Close, and the removal of a commemorative tree. I accept that may be outside the type of casework he usually handles. That is why a short, honest reply — even if only to say the questions sit with named officers, and to pass the tree query to the correct department — would have been sufficient. Silence is not.

Recorded approaches to Councillor Carroll ([email redacted]<[email redacted]>)

All sent. No substantive reply on any of them.

- 16 February 2026 — “Title Fraud and Procedural Concealment – Church View Close, Llandough (formerly Great House Farm / Ty Mawr)”. Planning and record-keeping gaps; 1988 demolition.
- 4 May 2026 — follow-up on BP v Buckler 1987; ITV footage; request for attention as Llandough councillor.
- 3 May 2026 — joined the public “George Carroll for Llandough” Facebook group (approved). Not a substitute for a council-email reply.
- 9 May 2026 — a wider formal notice also addressed to [email redacted]<[email redacted]>. That address bounced. Subsequent mail used the correct gdcarroll@ address.
- 7 June 2026 — “Church View Close, Llandough”. 1988 events from public records, family testimony and media.
- 25 June 2026 — “Great House Farm, Llandough”. Asked whether he had reviewed the earlier concerns and whether any discussion was possible.
- 13 July 2026 — “Great House Farm / Church View Close”. Full timeline restated. Ten-working-day request. Explicit question: who removed the tree my great-grandfather planted to commemorate the ownership claim, as shown in the Collection of Wales archive image.
- 27 July 2026 — formal complaint to [email redacted]<[email redacted]>, copied to Councillor Carroll, Democratic Services and the Monitoring Officer.
- 28 August 2026 — further letter to Councillor Carroll and Stephen Doughty MP on the same site.

What I am asking you to do

1. Note that the ward member has not answered, and that the complaint process produced no requirement that he do so.

2. Ask Councillor Carroll, or the relevant Director, to provide a short written reply on the tree: which department or landowner authorised or carried out its removal, on what date, and under what power or works order — or to confirm that the Council holds no such record.

3. Identify the correct officer contact for heritage, trees and historic planning records at Church View Close / former Great House Farm, so I am not left circling a silent ward inbox.

4. Confirm whether the Council will treat a documented family connection to a demolished historic farmstead in the ward as a legitimate basis for a reply, even where the correspondent is not presently resident in Llandough.

The thesis of my concern is that the lawfare/ warfare that systematically attempted to make our occupancy permissive as early as the 40's (with my grandmothers statement of title being stolen, a failed attempt to get us into a tenancy afterwards, and ambiguity in a 1955 order for another parcel we leased and defaulted on, which later meant it was able to be misinterpreted to make it appear our parcel of land (now Church View Close) was part of theirs, like it was in 1916 - 1928) is a racket. The ownership dispute was a problem created. The reaction followed and the solution was to focus on possession. And so in 1987 BP were awarded possession with what was a defective title chain.

I do not expect you to reopen 1987 litigation. I do expect the authority, once the ward member has been given months and a formal complaint, to answer a factual question about a tree on land in that ward. Because that tree was part of a long list of evidence supporting our ownership claim.

I can supply the original emails and the 27 July complaint in full if Democratic Services does not already have them. See attached the aforementioned tree planting ceremy image. I also enclose a draft chancery court allocation so you can understand the legal arguments.

Due to a lot of suspicious and conveniently timed deaths in our family, surrounding this case, like my grandmother dying in the 2 weeks she will have had to challenge BP quietly registering our land parcel in their names in 1983, without declaring our ownership claim, which was never exstinguished as the first 1974 court case was ajourned. Or my fathers death after his appeal of the 1987 ruling was dismissed on grounds of "heads BP win, tails we lose". Followed by ECHR rejection citing BP own the land, despite BP only seeking possession and never seeking or gaining ownership.

I have a trove of evidence and I am collecting more and investigating and in talks with CPS and Fraud Police and MoJ and Land Registry. The initial thing I would like from you is the record of the removal of the tree we planted. The picture attached depicts its location. I'd like to know who removed it and when it was removed?

Regards,

Sion Hywel Buckler (Ret'd Sergeant)
Royal Signals Cyber/ Electronic Warfare Professional and Life Member
[address redacted], Dinas Powys, [postcode redacted]

Mr Wigley,
I am writing to make a formal complaint to Cadw concerning the handling and substantive response to my correspondence regarding Great House Farm (Tŷ Mawr), Llandough, and particularly Cadw's 1988 consideration of whether the building should
 be protected by listing.
I am making this complaint directly to Cadw at this stage because I consider that Cadw should be given a proper opportunity to review and address the matters before any escalation to the wider Welsh Government complaints process.
For the avoidance of doubt, I am not making a further Freedom of Information request and I am not simply asking Cadw to produce records which it has already said no longer exist. I accept that Cadw has stated that all records it currently
 holds concerning the 1988 listing decision have been released.
My complaint concerns what can properly be established from the surviving evidence, whether the responses I have received have adequately addressed that evidence, and whether the historical record can now be described accurately where the underlying file
 has been lost.
1. The newly identified 1982 evidence
I have now identified a 1 October 1982 consultation letter from the Glamorgan-Gwent Archaeological Trust concerning the East Vale Local Plan and the proposed Ty Maw Farm site, identified as
H2.1.
The letter states:

“Ty Maw Farm (H2.1) is designated as a three-acre residential site. As you will see from the enclosed information the settlement at Llandough developed considerably from farming and fishing... Recent excavations at Llandough by the Trust revealed early occupation,
 part of the villa and medieval grange buildings. There remains a possibility that occupation continues to the north of the church; provision should be made, therefore, for thorough investigative work prior to the development.”

I do not suggest that this document, by itself, establishes that the standing farmhouse was required to be listed.
Its significance is narrower and more demonstrable: six years before the 1988 demolition, the archaeological and planning system already contained site-specific information identifying Ty Maw Farm as a proposed development site and recording substantial
 archaeological sensitivity in the immediate Llandough area, including possible continued occupation north of the church.
That materially affects the historical context in which Cadw's 1988 assessment needs to be understood.
I therefore ask Cadw to address:


Whether this 1982 information was held by, available to, or capable of being obtained by Cadw in the period leading to the 1988 decision.

Whether Cadw has any surviving evidence showing what archaeological, planning or historic-building information was available to the inspectors or decision-makers in 1988.

Whether there was communication between Cadw and the relevant planning/archaeological authorities concerning the proposed development of Ty Maw Farm and the need for investigation or protection.

If it is no longer possible to establish whether this evidence was actually considered, whether Cadw will expressly acknowledge that uncertainty rather than treating the absence of the historic file as evidence that the relevant information was absent.

2. The 1974 RCAHMW survey
I have previously drawn Cadw's attention to the 26 April 1974 Royal Commission survey by H.J. Thomas at ST16817331.
That survey recorded Great House Farm as a historic building, including features such as the late seventeenth-century character of the house, its cross-passage arrangement, adze-worked beams, ogee stops and barrel-vaulted cellar.
Cadw has stated that only two photographs from its relevant historic material survive and that it cannot now establish whether the 1974 survey was taken into account in the 1988 listing consideration.
I accept that this may now be incapable of being proved from the surviving file.
However, there is an important distinction between:
“Cadw cannot now establish whether the information was considered”
and
“there is no evidence that the information was available or relevant.”
The surviving RCAHMW material demonstrates that professional historic-building recording existed well before the 1988 decision.
I therefore ask Cadw to address specifically whether that material was available to Cadw through the inter-agency heritage system at the time and, if so, what can now be established about its availability.
3. Cadw's own evidence that listing was actively being considered in 1988
The surviving contemporary material indicates that in December 1988 Cadw was actively considering emergency protection/spot-listing of Great House Farm, including inspection and consultation concerning the building's historic significance.
That is important because it demonstrates that this was not retrospectively invented as a heritage issue decades later. Cadw itself was considering protection immediately before the building was demolished.
Cadw's present position is that the historical listing file no longer survives and that its retention arrangements at the time cannot now be established with certainty.
I am not asking Cadw to speculate about what a destroyed file contained.
I am asking Cadw to distinguish clearly between:

what the surviving evidence positively establishes;what information was demonstrably available by 1988;what actions by Cadw in 1988 can still be established;what cannot now be established because the historic record has been lost; andany conclusions Cadw considers cannot responsibly be drawn.
That distinction is particularly important when assessing whether the surviving record provides a sufficiently reliable account of what happened.
4. The planning authority and temporary protection
I also wish to clarify the position concerning temporary protection.
I am not suggesting that Cadw itself necessarily possessed the statutory power to serve a Building Preservation Notice. I understand that such protection was a matter for the relevant local planning authority under the legislation then in force.
The question for Cadw is therefore whether, during the 1988 consideration, 
Cadw advised, discussed or communicated with the relevant planning authority concerning any available temporary protection mechanism or the need to prevent demolition pending consideration of listing.
If Cadw cannot establish what was discussed because the records no longer survive, that should be stated expressly.
5. The later description of Great House Farm as “a listed building”
I have also identified later archaeological/planning documentation in which the former site is described in terms including:

“The site formerly contained Great House Farm (a listed building).”

I am not asserting that this wording conclusively proves that Great House Farm was formally listed at that time.
I am asking Cadw to explain, insofar as the surviving evidence permits, whether there is any known provenance for that description and whether Cadw considers it accurate, erroneous, or simply impossible now to determine.
This is relevant because it illustrates the existence of potentially conflicting historical accounts concerning the building's protection status.
6. The significance of the loss of the 1988 record
Cadw has understandably stated that the historic file cannot now be produced.
However, the loss of that file creates a historical evidential limitation; it should not automatically resolve questions arising from the surviving evidence in Cadw's favour.
The appropriate conclusion may simply be that some aspects of the 1988 decision
cannot now be reconstructed with certainty.
I would therefore like Cadw to consider whether its previous responses have drawn that distinction sufficiently clearly.
7. What I am asking Cadw to do
I am asking Cadw to treat this as a formal complaint and provide a substantive response addressing the following:
A. Whether the newly identified 1982 GGAT evidence materially changes Cadw's understanding of the information environment surrounding Ty Maw Farm before the 1988 demolition.
B. Whether Cadw can establish that the 1974 RCAHMW survey was available to it in 1988.
C. Whether Cadw can establish what archaeological, planning and historic-building information was available to its officers when the building was being considered for protection.
D. What can now be established about Cadw's communications with the local planning authority and other heritage bodies during the 1988 listing consideration.
E. Whether temporary protection was discussed or advised upon and, if not capable of being established, whether Cadw will state that plainly.
F. What can be established about the inspection of Great House Farm and the ultimate listing decision.
G. Whether Cadw accepts that the loss of the historic file means that some aspects of the 1988 decision can no longer be reconstructed reliably.
H. Whether Cadw considers the surviving documentary evidence, including the 1974 survey and 1982 archaeological/planning evidence, should be reflected in any relevant contemporary heritage record or historical account.
I. Whether Cadw can explain the provenance, insofar as it is capable of doing so, of the later description of the former site as containing “a listed building.”
J. Whether Cadw considers that its previous responses have adequately distinguished between the absence of surviving evidence and evidence that something did not happen.
8. Scope of this complaint
I want to be clear that I am not asking Cadw to determine my family's wider property or title claims, nor am I asking Cadw to reach a predetermined conclusion about the historical ownership of the land.
Those matters are separate.
This complaint is confined to Cadw's own heritage-related role, the 1988 protection/listing process, the information that can now be established as having existed, and the adequacy and accuracy of Cadw's present explanation of that history.
I am also not asking Cadw to speculate about missing documents. On the contrary, I ask that the absence of those documents be treated as an evidential limitation and expressly identified as such.
9. Requested outcome
I would like Cadw to:


Register this as a formal complaint and provide a complaint reference.

Have the matter reviewed by an appropriate person who has not simply repeated the previous FOI position.

Provide a point-by-point response to the matters above, taking account of the newly identified 1982 evidence.

Correct or clarify any part of Cadw's previous correspondence that is found to have been incomplete, inaccurate or insufficiently qualified.

State clearly which matters can now be established, which cannot, and which remain uncertain because the historical records no longer survive.

I regard that as a proportionate and reasonable opportunity for Cadw to address the matter directly before I consider whether escalation through the Welsh Government complaints process is necessary.
Yours sincerely,

Sion Buckler (Ret'd Sergeant)

Mr Wigley,

I am writing to make a *formal complaint to Cadw* concerning the handling
and substantive response to my correspondence regarding Great House Farm
(Tŷ Mawr), Llandough, and particularly Cadw's 1988 consideration of whether
the building should be protected by listing.

I am making this complaint directly to Cadw at this stage because I
consider that Cadw should be given a proper opportunity to review and
address the matters before any escalation to the wider Welsh Government
complaints process.

For the avoidance of doubt, I am *not making a further Freedom of
Information request* and I am not simply asking Cadw to produce records
which it has already said no longer exist. I accept that Cadw has stated
that all records it currently holds concerning the 1988 listing decision
have been released.

My complaint concerns what can properly be established from the surviving
evidence, whether the responses I have received have adequately addressed
that evidence, and whether the historical record can now be described
accurately where the underlying file has been lost.
1. The newly identified 1982 evidence

I have now identified a 1 October 1982 consultation letter from the
Glamorgan-Gwent Archaeological Trust concerning the East Vale Local Plan
and the proposed Ty Maw Farm site, identified as *H2.1*.

The letter states:

“Ty Maw Farm (H2.1) is designated as a three-acre residential site. As you
will see from the enclosed information the settlement at Llandough
developed considerably from farming and fishing... Recent excavations at
Llandough by the Trust revealed early occupation, part of the villa and
medieval grange buildings. There remains a possibility that occupation
continues to the north of the church; provision should be made, therefore,
for thorough investigative work prior to the development.”

I do not suggest that this document, by itself, establishes that the
standing farmhouse was required to be listed.

Its significance is narrower and more demonstrable: *six years before the
1988 demolition, the archaeological and planning system already contained
site-specific information identifying Ty Maw Farm as a proposed development
site and recording substantial archaeological sensitivity in the immediate
Llandough area, including possible continued occupation north of the
church.*

That materially affects the historical context in which Cadw's 1988
assessment needs to be understood.

I therefore ask Cadw to address:

   1.

   Whether this 1982 information was held by, available to, or capable of
   being obtained by Cadw in the period leading to the 1988 decision.
   2.

   Whether Cadw has any surviving evidence showing what archaeological,
   planning or historic-building information was available to the inspectors
   or decision-makers in 1988.
   3.

   Whether there was communication between Cadw and the relevant
   planning/archaeological authorities concerning the proposed development of
   Ty Maw Farm and the need for investigation or protection.
   4.

   If it is no longer possible to establish whether this evidence was
   actually considered, whether Cadw will expressly acknowledge that
   uncertainty rather than treating the absence of the historic file as
   evidence that the relevant information was absent.

2. The 1974 RCAHMW survey

I have previously drawn Cadw's attention to the 26 April 1974 Royal
Commission survey by H.J. Thomas at ST16817331.

That survey recorded Great House Farm as a historic building, including
features such as the late seventeenth-century character of the house, its
cross-passage arrangement, adze-worked beams, ogee stops and barrel-vaulted
cellar.

Cadw has stated that only two photographs from its relevant historic
material survive and that it cannot now establish whether the 1974 survey
was taken into account in the 1988 listing consideration.

I accept that this may now be incapable of being proved from the surviving
file.

However, there is an important distinction between:

*“Cadw cannot now establish whether the information was considered”*

and

*“there is no evidence that the information was available or relevant.”*

The surviving RCAHMW material demonstrates that professional
historic-building recording existed well before the 1988 decision.

I therefore ask Cadw to address specifically whether that material was
available to Cadw through the inter-agency heritage system at the time and,
if so, what can now be established about its availability.
3. Cadw's own evidence that listing was actively being considered in 1988

The surviving contemporary material indicates that in December 1988 Cadw
was actively considering emergency protection/spot-listing of Great House
Farm, including inspection and consultation concerning the building's
historic significance.

That is important because it demonstrates that this was not retrospectively
invented as a heritage issue decades later. Cadw itself was considering
protection immediately before the building was demolished.

Cadw's present position is that the historical listing file no longer
survives and that its retention arrangements at the time cannot now be
established with certainty.

I am not asking Cadw to speculate about what a destroyed file contained.

I am asking Cadw to distinguish clearly between:

   - what the surviving evidence positively establishes;
   - what information was demonstrably available by 1988;
   - what actions by Cadw in 1988 can still be established;
   - what cannot now be established because the historic record has been
   lost; and
   - any conclusions Cadw considers cannot responsibly be drawn.

That distinction is particularly important when assessing whether the
surviving record provides a sufficiently reliable account of what happened.
4. The planning authority and temporary protection

I also wish to clarify the position concerning temporary protection.

I am not suggesting that Cadw itself necessarily possessed the statutory
power to serve a Building Preservation Notice. I understand that such
protection was a matter for the relevant local planning authority under the
legislation then in force.

The question for Cadw is therefore whether, during the 1988
consideration, *Cadw
advised, discussed or communicated with the relevant planning authority
concerning any available temporary protection mechanism or the need to
prevent demolition pending consideration of listing.*

If Cadw cannot establish what was discussed because the records no longer
survive, that should be stated expressly.
5. The later description of Great House Farm as “a listed building”

I have also identified later archaeological/planning documentation in which
the former site is described in terms including:

“The site formerly contained Great House Farm (a listed building).”

I am not asserting that this wording conclusively proves that Great House
Farm was formally listed at that time.

I am asking Cadw to explain, insofar as the surviving evidence permits,
whether there is any known provenance for that description and whether Cadw
considers it accurate, erroneous, or simply impossible now to determine.

This is relevant because it illustrates the existence of potentially
conflicting historical accounts concerning the building's protection status.
6. The significance of the loss of the 1988 record

Cadw has understandably stated that the historic file cannot now be
produced.

However, the loss of that file creates a historical evidential limitation;
it should not automatically resolve questions arising from the surviving
evidence in Cadw's favour.

The appropriate conclusion may simply be that some aspects of the 1988
decision *cannot now be reconstructed with certainty*.

I would therefore like Cadw to consider whether its previous responses have
drawn that distinction sufficiently clearly.
7. What I am asking Cadw to do

I am asking Cadw to treat this as a formal complaint and provide a
substantive response addressing the following:

*A.* Whether the newly identified 1982 GGAT evidence materially changes
Cadw's understanding of the information environment surrounding Ty Maw Farm
before the 1988 demolition.

*B.* Whether Cadw can establish that the 1974 RCAHMW survey was available
to it in 1988.

*C.* Whether Cadw can establish what archaeological, planning and
historic-building information was available to its officers when the
building was being considered for protection.

*D.* What can now be established about Cadw's communications with the local
planning authority and other heritage bodies during the 1988 listing
consideration.

*E.* Whether temporary protection was discussed or advised upon and, if not
capable of being established, whether Cadw will state that plainly.

*F.* What can be established about the inspection of Great House Farm and
the ultimate listing decision.

*G.* Whether Cadw accepts that the loss of the historic file means that
some aspects of the 1988 decision can no longer be reconstructed reliably.

*H.* Whether Cadw considers the surviving documentary evidence, including
the 1974 survey and 1982 archaeological/planning evidence, should be
reflected in any relevant contemporary heritage record or historical
account.

*I.* Whether Cadw can explain the provenance, insofar as it is capable of
doing so, of the later description of the former site as containing “a
listed building.”

*J.* Whether Cadw considers that its previous responses have adequately
distinguished between the absence of surviving evidence and evidence that
something did not happen.
8. Scope of this complaint

I want to be clear that I am not asking Cadw to determine my family's wider
property or title claims, nor am I asking Cadw to reach a predetermined
conclusion about the historical ownership of the land.

Those matters are separate.

This complaint is confined to *Cadw's own heritage-related role, the 1988
protection/listing process, the information that can now be established as
having existed, and the adequacy and accuracy of Cadw's present explanation
of that history.*

I am also not asking Cadw to speculate about missing documents. On the
contrary, I ask that the absence of those documents be treated as an
evidential limitation and expressly identified as such.
9. Requested outcome

I would like Cadw to:

   1.

   Register this as a formal complaint and provide a complaint reference.
   2.

   Have the matter reviewed by an appropriate person who has not simply
   repeated the previous FOI position.
   3.

   Provide a point-by-point response to the matters above, taking account
   of the newly identified 1982 evidence.
   4.

   Correct or clarify any part of Cadw's previous correspondence that is
   found to have been incomplete, inaccurate or insufficiently qualified.
   5.

   State clearly which matters can now be established, which cannot, and
   which remain uncertain because the historical records no longer survive.

I regard that as a proportionate and reasonable opportunity for Cadw to
address the matter directly before I consider whether escalation through
the Welsh Government complaints process is necessary.

Yours sincerely,

*Sion Buckler (Ret'd Sergeant)*
